Detailed simulations show that inter-tank structural supports can create significant conduction paths from the outer tank to the inner tank, and will require innovative solutions and optimization to minimize thermal losses while providing the required mechanical support. Figure 15 shows that with minimal boss and support losses, the boil-off targets for Phase 2 tank can be met. Figure 16 shows high-fidelity model of the tank with structural features (inter-tank supports), and it is seen that the supports serve as paths for heat leak. Several tank support topologies were being evaluated to reduce heat leak. The intent of these concepts is to minimize the support cross-sectional areas while increasing the length of the conduction path. The assembly and interference of the supports with the multi-layer insulation (MLI) also need to be considered. The connections to external pipes also need to be properly insulated to minimize thermal losses. Figure 17 shows the effect of boss and inter-tank supports as a path for heat leak, and the resulting increase in boil-off. Slosh modeling: A preliminary model to capture slosh behavior of LH2 was created in ANSYS/Fluent for the Phase 1 tank (Figure 18). This is a two-phase volume-of-fluids based model and will be exercised to evaluate generic slosh mitigation concepts in the current quarter. Figure 19 shows the sloshing of LH2 in the Phase I tank, subject to a lateral sinusoidal 1G acceleration without baffles (left), and with baffles (right). While not optimized, the baffles help reduce the sloshing amplitude. This model demonstrates the capability to model sloshing. It is anticipated that baffle design and placement needed in a conformal tank will be different, but modeling of sloshing in the current geometry provides a baseline understanding of the response of LH2 under sinusoidal ‘g’ forces. Subsequent models will incorporate the g-force profile experienced by heavy-duty trucks, and with different placement of baffles, and study its impact on sloshing reduction. Manufacturing process: Inner tank manufacturing: With the final objective being to build a conformal composite tank, the tank design involves convex and concave surface features. Two major existing automated composite processes, filament winding (FW) and automated fiber placement (AFP) were considered for the inner tank manufacturing. In FW, as shown in Figure 20(a), the wet fiber tow will bridge across a concave surface feature and forms air-gap defects in the composite, instead of conforming to the concaved surface. However, in AFP, as shown in Figure 20(b), the roller are able to press tacky prepreg tapes onto various surfaces and the tacky tapes adhere to the previously placed prepreg surface.
